zh:
一阵微风吹过，铁锈和灰尘的气味里，隐约夹杂着一丝熟悉的化学药剂味。我不由得把早上发现的线索在脑中过了一遍：湿拖把、被蹭掉的青苔、呛人的除草剂味、蔫黄的草甸和盆栽……这下都说得通了，所有线索都指向保洁阿姨早上的大扫除，原来那种说不清的糟糕感觉，不过是空气中残留的、过量的除草剂。

等等——除草？这个词像钩子一样，从我记忆里拽出另一件事。 上上周三体育课，我溜上天台，怀里揣着一颗从花店弃置袋里捡来的铃兰种球。店员说它基本发不了芽，我却抱着一种天真的侥幸心理，将它埋入草甸，还为它细心盖上了一小片草皮。阿姨今天这般大肆清理，我那点脆弱的幻想，恐怕……

不敢再想下去了。我需要立刻去把那块土翻开，看个究竟。六楼天台的风里带着铁锈味。我跪在花圃前，汗水从额头上冒出来，上上周三下午四点零八分，我用自己的小拇指量着深度，把一枚铃兰的种球悄悄埋进这方土里。现在它居然……破土了，两片细小的叶片像合拢的书页，依偎着破土而出，这一瞬间的发现让我忘记了时间，也忘记了危险。正当我出神时——“叮铃铃！！！”下课铃声如同惊雷炸响，紧接着，催命般的跑操铃便接踵而至。

糟了！一听到这铃声，我顿时冷汗直流——这周是班主任亲自查勤！要是被发现不在，后果不堪设想。我猛地起身就要往回冲，连手上的泥都顾不上甩掉，就在转身要跑的刹那，铁门外突然传来对话声："小陈啊，我今天上来看看天台的定期维修情况。"，"护栏已经修好了，至于青苔，还是您考虑得周到，今天一早我特意安排了李阿姨上来清理干净了……"是教导主任！我的心瞬间冰凉。我转身就往上来时的铁门跑。冰冷的金属门把手硌得我掌心生疼。“哐当！” 我几乎是撞开门，跌进昏暗的楼梯间。

阴冷的、带着灰尘味的空气扑面而来。就在我以为只要跑得够快就能逃过一劫的瞬间，脚踝却猛地一紧——是那块我上来时卡住铁门的扁石头！“咔嚓——！” 我像一截被伐倒的木头，完全失控地向前扑去。我试图抓住什么，但只有空气掠过指缝，接着便是无可挽回地沿着陡峭的楼梯翻滚。肩膀、背部、腰部撞击着水泥台阶，视野天旋地转，失重感如潮水般漫过头顶，最后沉重地摔在底层，我的视野瞬间暗下，鲜红色的液体滑过额角。
en:
A light breeze swept past. Beneath the smells of rust and dust, there was the faint trace of a familiar chemical odor. I could not help replaying the clues I had found that morning: the wet mop, the moss rubbed away, the choking stench of herbicide, the wilted yellow patch of grass and the potted plants… Now it all made sense. Every clue pointed to the janitor’s thorough cleanup earlier in the day. That vague, unsettling feeling was nothing more than the residue of an excessive amount of weed killer lingering in the air.

But wait—weed killer?

The word hooked into my memory and yanked up something else. The Wednesday before last, during P.E., I had slipped up to the rooftop with a lily-of-the-valley bulb tucked against my chest—something I had fished out of a florist’s discard bag. The clerk had said it would never really sprout, but I clung to a naïve hope anyway. I buried it in the grass patch, even carefully covering it with a small piece of turf. With the janitor cleaning so aggressively today, my fragile little fantasy was probably…

I did not dare finish the thought. I needed to dig up that spot immediately and see for myself.

The wind on the sixth-floor rooftop carried the taste of rust. I knelt by the flowerbed, sweat beading on my forehead. Wednesday before last at 4:08 p.m., I had measured the depth with my pinky and quietly buried a lily-of-the-valley bulb in this soil. And now it actually…

It had broken through.

Two tiny leaves—like book pages pressed together—nestled against each other as they pushed up from the earth. The discovery made me forget time, and it made me forget danger. Just as I stood there, entranced—

Ding-ling-ling!!!

The end-of-class bell exploded like thunder. Then, right on its heels, came the relentless drill bell, driving everyone outside.

Crap.

The moment I heard it, cold sweat flooded my back—this week the homeroom teacher was personally checking attendance. If I got caught missing, the consequences would be unthinkable. I shot to my feet and lunged toward the stairs, not even bothering to shake the dirt from my hands. But in the instant I turned to run, voices rose outside the iron door:

“Chen, I’m coming up to check the rooftop’s scheduled maintenance.”

“The railing’s been fixed. As for the moss, you were right to be cautious—early this morning I specifically arranged for Auntie Li to come up and clean it thoroughly…”

It was the dean.

My blood turned to ice. I spun and sprinted for the iron door I had come through. The cold metal handle bit into my palm.

Clang!

I practically rammed the door open and stumbled into the dim stairwell.

A chill, dust-laced air hit my face. In that moment—when I thought that if I ran fast enough I could still escape—something cinched tight around my ankle.

The flat stone.

The one I had jammed under the door when I came up.

Crack—

Like a felled log, I pitched forward, utterly out of control. I tried to grab onto something, but only air slipped through my fingers. The next instant was irreversible: I was tumbling down the steep stairs. My shoulder, my back, my waist slammed against concrete steps. The world spun. Weightlessness surged like a tide over my head.

And then I hit the bottom—hard.

My vision went dark at once, and a bright red line of liquid slid down from my temple.

zh:
故事概要：

吱——嘎——

生锈的铁门发出刺耳的摩擦声，像刀子划过耳膜，在空荡荡的楼梯间里不断回荡。

这个点……应该没人吧？

我小心翼翼地侧身挤进半开的铁门，迅速回身将刚捡的扁石头卡在门缝下，心还悬在五楼那个差点撞见教务主任的转角——这扇门要是被风吹上锁死，我就真被困在这里了。环顾四周，空荡荡的天台上只有我的影子被阳光拉长。我松了口气，抬手擦了擦额角的薄汗。

没错，因为听不进去课，我又逃课了。

和往常一样，在八点十分准时出门，我接过老妈递来的早餐，对正在系领带的老爸说了声"走了"。踏进校门时，晨读铃正好打响。我溜进教室，把书包往座位上一扔，翻开笔记本假装复习。当老师低头翻阅领读教材时，我立即皱起眉捂住肚子，猫着腰从后门溜了出去——这一套操作，我实在是太熟练了。

天台在主教学楼的顶层，得爬六层楼才能到。底下的一到四楼都是教室，五楼是行政办公室，平时除了老师，学生很少上来。而六楼，更是被遗忘的角落，偶尔只有保洁阿姨拖着扫把经过，或是外校的访客进来参观。这个被遗忘的地方，其实比想象中开阔。站在银灰色的护栏边，能看到整个校园的景色，繁茂的花圃里，成片的鲜黄色花朵在其中静静绽放。中间摆着几张掉漆的长椅，没人打理，椅脚与周围的水泥地面上，都覆上了一层斑驳的青苔。

一阵风吹来，却带着一股说不上来的怪味。我皱眉看向不远处的铁皮公告栏：边角已经磨得有点破了，但整体依旧十分牢固。走近时，消毒水混杂着霉味扑鼻而来，呛得人喉咙发紧。栏板上写着“为保安全，请勿倚靠或攀爬防护栏”。字迹被淡绿色的青苔遮住了一部分，偏偏有几处像是被人硬生生蹭掉了，露出底下深色的秃斑。总觉得哪里不太对——这味道，我好像在哪闻过。

带着这份疑惑，我决定按照日记里提到的线索，把天台仔细查看一遍。刚一转身，就注意到花圃边靠着一把滴水的拖把和半瓶除草剂。瓶身摸上去冰凉，瓶口传来的刺鼻的药剂味，和拖把的霉味混在一起，直冲鼻腔。我晃了晃瓶身，里面只剩一半，看这情形，保洁阿姨早上肯定来过，而且用量不小。顺着日记的提示，我走到旁边那片草甸。那里几乎看不出有人打理过的痕迹，只有一堆叫不出名字的野草乱糟糟地长着，消毒水、霉变和土壤腐败的气味在这里异常浓烈，简直像个小型的生态灾难现场。再看旁边并排的三盆植物，同样显得不太健康。
en:
Story Summary:

Creak—Screech—

The rusty iron door let out a shrill grinding sound, like a blade scraping across the eardrum, echoing again and again through the empty stairwell.

At this hour… there should be no one here, right?

I cautiously squeezed sideways through the half-open door, then quickly turned back and wedged a flat stone I had just picked up into the gap. My nerves were still taut from the corner on the fifth floor where I had nearly run into the dean—if the wind slammed this door shut and locked it, I would be trapped up here for good. I scanned the surroundings. The rooftop was completely deserted, the only thing there being my shadow stretched long in the sunlight. I let out a breath and raised a hand to wipe the thin sheen of sweat from my forehead.

That is right: because I could not concentrate in class, I cut school again.

As usual, I left home on time at 8:10. I took the breakfast my mother handed me and called out “I’m leaving” to my father, who was fastening his tie. When I stepped through the school gate, the morning reading bell rang at that exact moment. I slipped into the classroom, tossed my backpack onto my seat, and opened my notebook to pretend I was reviewing. The instant the teacher lowered their head to flip through the recitation materials, I immediately furrowed my brow, clutched my stomach, and hunched my way out through the back door—this routine, I have become far too familiar with.

The rooftop sits on top of the main teaching building; it takes six flights of stairs to reach it. The first through fourth floors are classrooms, the fifth floor is administrative offices, and students rarely come up there except teachers are around. The sixth floor, even more so, is a forgotten corner—at most, a janitor might pass by dragging a mop, or an outside visitor might wander in on a tour. This forgotten place is more spacious than one might expect. Standing by the silvery-gray railing, you can take in the entire campus: in the flourishing flowerbeds,大片 of bright yellow blossoms bloom quietly. A few long benches with peeling paint sit in the middle, unattended; both the bench legs and the surrounding cement are coated with mottled patches of moss.

A gust of wind blew through, carrying a strange odor I could not quite place. Frowning, I looked toward a sheet-metal bulletin board not far away. The corners were worn, but the structure was still sturdy. As I drew closer, the mixed stench of disinfectant and mildew hit me head-on, tightening my throat with its sharpness. On the panel were the words: “For safety, please do not lean on or climb the protective railing.” Some of the lettering was obscured by pale green moss, yet in a few places it looked as though someone had forcibly rubbed it away, exposing dark, bare patches underneath. Something felt off—this smell, I am sure I have encountered it somewhere before.

With that suspicion in mind, I decided to follow the clues mentioned in the diary and examine the rooftop carefully. The moment I turned around, I noticed a dripping mop propped against the edge of a flowerbed, along with half a bottle of herbicide. The bottle felt cold to the touch. The pungent chemical odor rising from its mouth mixed with the musty smell of the mop and shot straight into my nose. I shook the bottle; only about half remained. Judging from this, the janitor must have been here in the morning—and used quite a lot.

Following the diary’s guidance, I walked over to a nearby patch of grass. There were almost no signs of maintenance—only a chaotic tangle of nameless weeds. The odors of disinfectant, mold, and rotting soil were unusually strong here, like the scene of a miniature ecological disaster. Beside it stood three potted plants lined up together, and they looked just as unhealthy.

zh:
在天台角落，一台亮着光的自动售货机格外显眼。我正觉得口干，凑近一看，最便宜的矿泉水也要三枚硬币。摸了摸空空的口袋，正失望时，却注意到碎石间有几朵黄色的小花——和花圃里的一样，大概是风把种子带到了这里。我注意到花影间有银光一闪，伸手拨开碎石，果真从泥土里拾起了一枚银色硬币。看来我今天的运气还算不错的。刚感到庆幸，就发现旁边碎石下也闪着微光。我伸手拨开，果然又找到一枚。起身时，我的视线扫到不远处一个湿漉漉的下水道口，，缝隙里好像也有什么在发亮。但扑面而来的异味和黏腻的污垢让我下意识退了一步。我本来想，为了一枚硬币弄脏手可不值得……可转念一想，让硬币在这种地方污染环境总归不好。对，是为了清理环境。这个念头说服了我。我迅速蹲下，用指甲从缝里小心地抠出了那枚硬币。

加上之前找到的，现在终于凑够三枚了。我迫不及待地走回售货机前，塞进硬币，按下矿泉水的按钮。水很凉，一下子就把喉咙里的干渴扑灭了。我靠在售货机旁，长长舒了口气，感觉原本紧绷的身体渐渐松弛，周围也安静下来了。真神奇，一瓶水而已，却好像把心里那块堵着的东西化开了。我转了转手里的空瓶，听着售货机的嗡鸣变远，看着光影在地面铺开，心情奇异地平静了。
en:
In a corner of the rooftop, a vending machine glowing with light stood out sharply against the dull surroundings. My throat felt dry, so I walked over—only to find that even the cheapest bottle of water cost three coins. I patted my pockets. Empty. Just as disappointment began to sink in, I noticed a few small yellow flowers among the gravel—the same kind as in the flowerbeds. The wind must have carried their seeds here.

Something flashed silver between the shadows of the petals. I reached down and brushed aside the stones. Sure enough, I picked a silver coin out of the dirt.

Looks like my luck isn’t so bad today.

I had barely finished feeling relieved when I spotted another faint glimmer under the gravel nearby. I cleared it away, and found a second coin.

As I stood up, my gaze flicked toward a damp drain a short distance away. Something seemed to be shining in the narrow gap there too. But the stench rushing up and the sticky grime made me instinctively step back. I thought, for a moment, that dirtying my hands for a single coin wasn’t worth it…

Then another thought followed close behind: letting a coin sit in a place like that and foul the environment probably wasn’t good either.

Yes—this is for cleaning up the environment.

That rationale convinced me. I crouched down quickly and used my fingernail to pry the coin out from the crack with careful, scraping motions.

With the ones I’d found earlier, I finally had three.

I hurried back to the vending machine, fed in the coins, and pressed the button for mineral water. The bottle was cold—so cold it instantly quenched the dryness in my throat. I leaned against the machine and let out a long breath. The tension in my body began to loosen, and the world around me seemed to quiet down.

It’s strange. It was only a bottle of water, and yet it felt as if something knotted inside my chest had melted away. I turned the empty bottle in my hand, listened as the vending machine’s hum receded into the background, watched light and shadow spread across the ground—

and felt, oddly, at peace.
